CHAPTER 18 - HOMEOSTASIS: THE STEADY STATE

Introduction

The cells of our body are extremely sensitive. They function properly only within a narrow range of temperature, water content, salt concentration, pH, glucose level and oxygen supply. Yet the world outside is constantly changing - it may be hot or cold, wet or dry, and the food we eat varies from meal to meal. How then do our cells enjoy such a stable environment? The answer is HOMEOSTASIS - the maintenance of a constant internal environment despite changes in the external surroundings. The word comes from the Greek 'homoios' (same) and 'stasis' (standing). Homeostasis does not mean an absolutely fixed condition; rather it is a DYNAMIC steady state in which variables are held within narrow limits around a set point by continuous self-regulating adjustments.

18.1 THE CONCEPT OF HOMEOSTASIS AND THE INTERNAL ENVIRONMENT

The great French physiologist CLAUDE BERNARD (1813-1878) first recognised that the cells of a complex animal are not directly exposed to the outside world. Instead they are bathed in a fluid he called the 'milieu interieur' or INTERNAL ENVIRONMENT. He famously stated that 'the constancy of the internal environment is the condition for a free and independent life'. It is this constancy that frees an animal from being a slave to its surroundings. Later, in the 1920s, the American physiologist WALTER CANNON studied how the body actively defends this constancy and coined the term HOMEOSTASIS for the coordinated processes that keep the internal environment steady.

What exactly is the internal environment? In a multicellular animal it is the EXTRACELLULAR FLUID that surrounds the cells. It has three connected parts. BLOOD PLASMA is the fluid part of blood that circulates in the vessels. TISSUE FLUID (interstitial fluid) leaks out of the capillaries and directly bathes every cell, supplying oxygen and nutrients and carrying away wastes. LYMPH is the excess tissue fluid that drains into lymphatic vessels and is eventually returned to the blood. Cells exchange materials with the tissue fluid, the tissue fluid exchanges with blood, and blood exchanges with the outside world through the lungs, gut, kidneys and skin. Because the cell never touches the changing outside world directly, keeping the internal environment constant is the same as keeping the cells' surroundings constant.

The main variables that homeostasis regulates are: body TEMPERATURE, the WATER and SALT balance (osmotic concentration), the concentration of GLUCOSE and other nutrients, the pH (acidity) of body fluids, the levels of oxygen and carbon dioxide, and the removal of nitrogenous wastes. Each of these is held near an optimum SET POINT.

18.2 FEEDBACK MECHANISMS AND CONTROL SYSTEMS

Homeostasis works through CONTROL SYSTEMS built on the principle of FEEDBACK. Every homeostatic control system has three components. A RECEPTOR (sensor) detects a change in the regulated variable and measures how far it has drifted from the set point. A CONTROL CENTRE (integrator), often in the brain or an endocrine gland, compares the information from the receptor against the set point and decides on the response. An EFFECTOR (muscle or gland) carries out the response that brings the variable back towards the set point.

NEGATIVE FEEDBACK is the most common mechanism in the body. Here the response OPPOSES or reverses the original change, so the variable is pushed back towards the set point. When a variable rises above the set point, negative feedback lowers it; when it falls below, negative feedback raises it. The result is stability - the variable oscillates gently around the set point. A familiar non-living analogy is a thermostat controlling a room heater: when the room gets too cold the thermostat switches the heater on, and when it gets warm enough it switches the heater off. Almost all homeostatic controls - temperature, blood glucose, water balance, blood pressure, pH - use negative feedback.

POSITIVE FEEDBACK is far less common. Here the response REINFORCES the original change, driving the variable further from the starting point rather than back to it. Positive feedback is used when a process must be pushed rapidly to completion. Examples include the surge of oxytocin that intensifies uterine contractions during CHILDBIRTH until the baby is delivered, the cascade of clotting factors during BLOOD CLOTTING, and the rising phase of a nerve impulse (the opening of sodium channels). Because positive feedback is inherently unstable, it is used only briefly and is usually shut off by an external event (such as birth).

18.3 THERMOREGULATION

THERMOREGULATION is the homeostatic control of body temperature. Temperature matters because the enzymes that run metabolism work best within a narrow range; too cold and reactions slow down, too hot and proteins denature.

Animals are classified by how they manage body temperature. ENDOTHERMS (also called HOMEOTHERMS or 'warm-blooded' animals) - birds and mammals - generate heat internally from their own metabolism and keep their body temperature nearly CONSTANT regardless of the surroundings. Human core temperature is held close to 37 degrees C. ECTOTHERMS (also called POIKILOTHERMS or 'cold-blooded' animals) - fishes, amphibians, reptiles and invertebrates - depend mainly on external sources of heat, so their body temperature VARIES with the environment. Ectotherms still regulate behaviourally, for example a lizard basking in the sun to warm up or moving into shade to cool down.

Heat is constantly exchanged with the surroundings by four physical routes: RADIATION (emission of heat as infrared waves), CONDUCTION (transfer to objects in direct contact), CONVECTION (transfer to moving air or water), and EVAPORATION (loss of heat when water, such as sweat, evaporates). Body temperature stays constant when heat gained from metabolism and the environment equals heat lost.

In mammals the SKIN is the main organ of temperature exchange and the HYPOTHALAMUS in the brain acts as the THERMOSTAT. The hypothalamus contains a thermoregulatory centre that senses the temperature of the blood flowing through it and also receives signals from temperature receptors in the skin. It compares the body temperature with the set point (about 37 degrees C) and triggers the appropriate responses through negative feedback.

RESPONSES TO COLD (when body temperature falls, the aim is to GAIN and CONSERVE heat): the skin arterioles constrict (VASOCONSTRICTION) so less warm blood reaches the surface and less heat is lost; SHIVERING - rapid involuntary muscle contractions - generates extra heat; the hair-erector muscles raise the body hairs (giving 'goose bumps') to trap an insulating layer of air; sweating stops; and the thyroid and adrenal glands may raise the metabolic rate to produce more heat.

RESPONSES TO HEAT (when body temperature rises, the aim is to LOSE heat): the skin arterioles dilate (VASODILATION) so more warm blood flows near the surface and heat radiates away, flushing the skin; the SWEAT GLANDS secrete sweat, whose evaporation cools the body; and behaviour changes, such as seeking shade and reducing activity. Together these responses form a negative-feedback loop that keeps core temperature steady.

FEVER is a controlled RAISING of the hypothalamic set point by chemicals called pyrogens released during infection; the body then works to hold the higher temperature, which helps fight pathogens. HYPOTHERMIA (dangerously low body temperature) and HYPERTHERMIA or heat stroke (dangerously high temperature) occur when these controls are overwhelmed.

18.4 OSMOREGULATION

OSMOREGULATION is the homeostatic control of the WATER and SALT (solute) content of the body fluids - that is, the regulation of their osmotic concentration. If cells lose too much water they shrink; if they gain too much they swell and may burst. So the osmotic concentration of the internal environment must be kept steady.

In humans and other mammals the KIDNEY is the principal osmoregulatory organ. By filtering the blood and then selectively reabsorbing water and salts, the kidney adjusts the volume and concentration of the urine to keep the blood osmotic concentration constant. Two hormones fine-tune this process by negative feedback. ADH (ANTIDIURETIC HORMONE, also called vasopressin), released from the posterior pituitary, makes the kidney tubules (collecting ducts) more permeable to water so that more water is REABSORBED and a smaller volume of concentrated urine is produced. When the blood becomes too concentrated (for example after sweating or drinking little), osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the rise and ADH secretion increases, conserving water. When the blood is too dilute, ADH falls and a large volume of dilute urine is passed. ALDOSTERONE, a hormone from the adrenal cortex, controls SALT balance by promoting the reabsorption of sodium ions (and with them, water) in the kidney tubules, which also helps regulate blood volume and pressure.

Different environments pose different osmotic problems. FRESHWATER ANIMALS live in surroundings more dilute than their body fluids, so water constantly enters their bodies by osmosis and salts tend to be lost; they cope by producing large amounts of dilute urine and actively taking up salts through their gills. MARINE BONY FISHES live in water saltier than their body fluids, so they tend to lose water and gain salt; they drink sea water, excrete salt through their gills, and pass only a small amount of concentrated urine. TERRESTRIAL ANIMALS face the constant danger of drying out (desiccation); they conserve water with waterproof skins, by producing concentrated urine (aided by ADH) and, in many, by excreting nitrogen as insoluble uric acid that needs little water.

18.5 REGULATION OF BLOOD GLUCOSE AND BLOOD pH

REGULATION OF BLOOD GLUCOSE: Glucose is the body's main fuel, and the brain in particular depends on a steady supply. The normal fasting level is about 70-110 mg per 100 mL of blood. Two hormones from the ISLETS OF LANGERHANS in the PANCREAS control it by negative feedback. INSULIN, from the beta cells, is released when blood glucose RISES (as after a meal); it LOWERS blood glucose by promoting the uptake of glucose into cells and its storage in the liver and muscles as GLYCOGEN (glycogenesis), and by promoting the conversion of glucose to fat. GLUCAGON, from the alpha cells, is released when blood glucose FALLS (as during fasting); it RAISES blood glucose by stimulating the liver to break down glycogen back into glucose (glycogenolysis) and to make new glucose. The two hormones act in opposite directions (they are ANTAGONISTIC), and together they hold blood glucose steady. Failure of this control causes DIABETES MELLITUS, in which insulin is lacking or ineffective and blood glucose rises dangerously high (hyperglycaemia), spilling into the urine.

REGULATION OF BLOOD pH: The enzymes and proteins of the body work only within a narrow pH range; human blood is kept close to pH 7.4 (slightly alkaline). Blood pH is defended in three ways. BUFFERS in the blood - chiefly the bicarbonate buffer system, along with proteins and phosphates - resist changes in pH by mopping up excess acid or base. The LUNGS remove carbon dioxide; because dissolved carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid, breathing out CO2 removes acid, and the rate of breathing is adjusted to control it (faster breathing removes more acid). The KIDNEYS provide the slow, long-term control by excreting excess hydrogen ions (acid) in the urine and reabsorbing or generating bicarbonate. Together these keep the blood pH within about 7.35 to 7.45.

18.6 HOMEOSTATIC ROLES OF ORGANS, EXCRETION AND DISORDERS

Several organs work together to maintain homeostasis, and the LIVER is one of the most versatile. Its homeostatic roles include: regulating blood glucose by storing and releasing glycogen (under insulin and glucagon); DEAMINATION of excess amino acids and converting the toxic ammonia produced into much less toxic UREA (the ornithine or urea cycle) for excretion; storing iron, vitamins and glycogen; producing plasma proteins such as albumin (which maintains blood osmotic pressure) and clotting factors; DETOXIFYING drugs, alcohol and other poisons; and generating heat that helps thermoregulation.

EXCRETION is itself a homeostatic process. By removing the nitrogenous wastes (urea, uric acid), excess salts, water and hydrogen ions, the excretory system - chiefly the KIDNEYS - simultaneously controls the water balance, the salt balance and the pH of the internal environment, in addition to clearing toxic wastes. Thus excretion is not merely 'throwing out rubbish'; it is central to keeping the internal environment constant.

DISORDERS OF HOMEOSTATIC FAILURE arise when a control system breaks down. DIABETES MELLITUS results from failure of blood-glucose control (lack or ineffectiveness of insulin). Kidney failure disrupts water, salt and pH balance and allows wastes to accumulate. Failure of temperature control leads to HYPOTHERMIA or HEAT STROKE. Disturbances of blood pH cause ACIDOSIS (blood too acidic) or ALKALOSIS (blood too alkaline), both dangerous. Dehydration disrupts osmotic balance. These disorders show, by their consequences, just how vital continuous homeostatic regulation is to life.

SUMMARY

- Homeostasis is the maintenance of a constant internal environment despite changes outside; it is a dynamic steady state around set points, not a fixed condition.
- Claude Bernard described the constant internal environment ('milieu interieur') as the condition for free life; Walter Cannon coined the term homeostasis.
- The internal environment is the extracellular fluid - blood plasma, tissue fluid and lymph - that bathes the cells.
- Control systems use a receptor, a control centre and an effector, and work mainly by NEGATIVE FEEDBACK, in which the response opposes the change and restores the set point. POSITIVE FEEDBACK (childbirth, blood clotting, nerve impulse) reinforces a change and is used briefly.
- Thermoregulation: endotherms/homeotherms (birds, mammals) keep a constant temperature by internal heat; ectotherms/poikilotherms vary with the environment. Heat is exchanged by radiation, conduction, convection and evaporation. The skin exchanges heat and the hypothalamus is the thermostat. Cold triggers vasoconstriction, shivering and hair erection; heat triggers vasodilation and sweating.
- Osmoregulation: the kidney regulates water and salt balance; ADH increases water reabsorption (concentrated urine) and aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption. Freshwater animals excrete dilute urine and take up salts; marine fishes drink sea water and excrete salt; terrestrial animals conserve water.
- Blood glucose is held near 70-110 mg/100 mL by antagonistic insulin (lowers it, stores glycogen) and glucagon (raises it, breaks down glycogen), via negative feedback; failure causes diabetes mellitus.
- Blood pH is held near 7.4 by buffers (bicarbonate), the lungs (removing CO2) and the kidneys (excreting H+).
- The liver has many homeostatic roles: glucose storage, urea formation from ammonia, plasma proteins, detoxification and heat. Excretion by the kidneys controls water, salt and pH balance.
- Homeostatic failure causes disorders such as diabetes mellitus, kidney failure, hypothermia, heat stroke, acidosis and alkalosis.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Homeostasis: The Steady State (NIOS Senior Secondary Biology)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Write concise, well-organised answers. For long-answer questions, name the organs and hormones involved and describe the feedback mechanism clearly.

questions.question: Define homeostasis and explain why it is described as a dynamic steady state rather than a fixed condition.
questions.answer: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a constant internal environment in the body in spite of changes in the external surroundings. It is called a dynamic steady state because the regulated variables (temperature, glucose, water, pH and so on) are not frozen at a single fixed value; instead they fluctuate gently within narrow limits around a set point. Continuous self-regulating adjustments constantly push each variable back towards its set point, so the overall condition stays steady even though small changes are always taking place.
questions.explanation: Definition plus the meaning of 'dynamic' - variables oscillate within narrow limits around a set point.

questions.question: Name the three parts of the internal environment and state the contribution of Claude Bernard and Walter Cannon.
questions.answer: The internal environment is the extracellular fluid and has three connected parts: (i) blood plasma, (ii) tissue (interstitial) fluid, and (iii) lymph. Claude Bernard first recognised that cells are bathed in a constant internal environment (the 'milieu interieur') and said its constancy is the condition for a free life. Walter Cannon later studied how the body actively defends this constancy and coined the term 'homeostasis'.
questions.explanation: Plasma, tissue fluid, lymph; Bernard - milieu interieur; Cannon - coined homeostasis.

questions.question: Distinguish between negative feedback and positive feedback, giving one example of each.
questions.answer: In negative feedback the response opposes (reverses) the original change and brings the variable back towards the set point, giving stability; for example, when blood glucose rises, insulin lowers it again. In positive feedback the response reinforces the original change, driving the variable further from the starting point; for example, during childbirth oxytocin intensifies uterine contractions until the baby is delivered. Negative feedback is the common homeostatic mechanism; positive feedback is used briefly to drive a process to completion.
questions.explanation: Opposes vs reinforces; example each (insulin/glucose vs childbirth).

questions.question: Describe how the human body responds to a fall in body temperature (cold) to restore its normal temperature. Name the control centre involved.
questions.answer: When the body is exposed to cold, temperature receptors in the skin and the thermoregulatory centre in the HYPOTHALAMUS (the body's thermostat) detect that the body temperature has fallen below the set point of about 37 C. By negative feedback the hypothalamus triggers responses that GAIN and CONSERVE heat: (i) the skin arterioles constrict (vasoconstriction), so less warm blood reaches the surface and less heat is lost; (ii) shivering begins - rapid involuntary muscle contractions that release heat; (iii) the hair-erector muscles raise the body hairs (goose bumps), trapping an insulating layer of air; (iv) sweating stops; and (v) the thyroid and adrenal glands may raise the metabolic rate to generate more heat. Together these raise the body temperature back to normal, at which point the responses are switched off.
questions.explanation: Hypothalamus as control centre; vasoconstriction, shivering, hair erection, reduced sweating, raised metabolism.

questions.question: Explain the role of ADH in osmoregulation.
questions.answer: ADH (antidiuretic hormone, or vasopressin) is released from the posterior pituitary when the blood becomes too concentrated (for example after sweating or drinking little water). Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the rise in osmotic concentration and increase ADH secretion. ADH makes the kidney tubules (collecting ducts) more permeable to water, so more water is reabsorbed back into the blood and a smaller volume of concentrated urine is produced. This conserves water and lowers the blood's osmotic concentration back towards normal. When the blood is too dilute, ADH falls and a large volume of dilute urine is passed.
questions.explanation: ADH increases water reabsorption in the collecting ducts, giving concentrated urine and conserving water.

questions.question: Explain how blood glucose is regulated by insulin and glucagon. Why are these hormones said to be antagonistic?
questions.answer: Blood glucose is normally held near 70-110 mg per 100 mL of blood by two hormones from the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas, working by negative feedback. After a meal, when blood glucose RISES, the beta cells release INSULIN. Insulin lowers blood glucose by promoting the uptake of glucose into cells and its storage in the liver and muscles as glycogen (glycogenesis) and its conversion to fat. During fasting, when blood glucose FALLS, the alpha cells release GLUCAGON. Glucagon raises blood glucose by stimulating the liver to break down glycogen into glucose (glycogenolysis) and to make new glucose. Because insulin lowers blood glucose while glucagon raises it, they act in OPPOSITE directions - they are said to be antagonistic. Their balanced, opposing actions keep blood glucose steady. Failure of this control (lack or ineffectiveness of insulin) causes diabetes mellitus.
questions.explanation: Insulin lowers (stores glycogen), glucagon raises (breaks glycogen); opposite actions = antagonistic.

questions.question: State three homeostatic roles of the liver.
questions.answer: Three homeostatic roles of the liver are: (i) regulating blood glucose by storing excess glucose as glycogen and releasing glucose when needed (under insulin and glucagon); (ii) converting the toxic ammonia produced by the deamination of excess amino acids into much less toxic urea for excretion; and (iii) detoxifying drugs, alcohol and other poisons. (Other roles include making plasma proteins and generating heat.)
questions.explanation: Any three: glucose/glycogen store, ammonia to urea, detoxification, plasma proteins, heat.

questions.question: How do the lungs and kidneys help to regulate the pH of the blood?
questions.answer: The lungs help regulate blood pH by removing carbon dioxide. Dissolved carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid in the blood, so breathing out CO2 removes acid; the rate of breathing is adjusted so that faster breathing removes more acid and raises pH. The kidneys provide slow, long-term control by excreting excess hydrogen ions (acid) in the urine and by reabsorbing or generating bicarbonate, which acts as a buffer. Together with the blood buffers they keep the blood pH close to 7.4 (within about 7.35 to 7.45).
questions.explanation: Lungs remove CO2 (acid) by breathing; kidneys excrete H+ and manage bicarbonate.

questions.question: Distinguish between endotherms (homeotherms) and ectotherms (poikilotherms) with one example of each.
questions.answer: Endotherms (homeotherms, 'warm-blooded' animals) generate heat internally from their own metabolism and keep their body temperature nearly constant regardless of the surroundings; examples are birds and mammals (such as humans). Ectotherms (poikilotherms, 'cold-blooded' animals) rely mainly on external sources of heat, so their body temperature varies with the environment; examples are fishes, amphibians and reptiles (such as a lizard). Ectotherms still regulate temperature behaviourally, for example by basking in the sun or moving into shade.
questions.explanation: Endotherm = internal heat, constant temp (birds/mammals); ectotherm = external heat, variable temp (reptiles).

questions.question: Explain what is meant by a disorder of homeostatic failure. Describe diabetes mellitus and one other example.
questions.answer: A disorder of homeostatic failure arises when a control system that normally keeps a variable near its set point breaks down, so the variable moves outside its safe range and harms the body. DIABETES MELLITUS is a failure of blood-glucose control: insulin is lacking or ineffective, so glucose is not taken up and stored properly and blood glucose rises dangerously high (hyperglycaemia), spilling into the urine and causing thirst, excess urination and long-term damage. Another example is failure of temperature control: if the thermoregulatory responses are overwhelmed, the body temperature falls too low (HYPOTHERMIA) or rises too high (heat stroke/HYPERTHERMIA), both of which can be fatal. (Other examples include kidney failure, which disrupts water, salt and pH balance, and acidosis or alkalosis, in which blood pH moves outside its normal range.) These disorders show how vital continuous homeostatic regulation is to life.
questions.explanation: Failure of a control system; diabetes = glucose control failure; hypothermia/heat stroke = temperature control failure.

questions.question: Define homeostasis.
questions.answer: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a constant internal environment in the body in spite of changes in the external surroundings. It is achieved by continuous self-regulating adjustments that keep variables such as temperature, glucose, water, salts and pH within narrow limits around their set points.
questions.explanation: Definition of homeostasis - constant internal environment.

questions.question: What is meant by the 'internal environment'? Name its parts.
questions.answer: The internal environment is the extracellular fluid that surrounds and bathes the cells of the body. It has three connected parts: blood plasma (the fluid in the blood vessels), tissue (interstitial) fluid (which directly bathes the cells), and lymph (excess tissue fluid drained into lymphatic vessels). Because cells never touch the changing outside world directly, keeping this fluid constant keeps the cells' surroundings constant.
questions.explanation: Extracellular fluid: plasma, tissue fluid, lymph.

questions.question: Why must the internal environment be kept constant?
questions.answer: The cells of the body function properly only within a narrow range of temperature, water content, salt concentration, pH, glucose and oxygen. Enzymes and other proteins work best under these conditions and are damaged outside them. Since cells are bathed in the internal environment and exchange materials with it, keeping the internal environment constant keeps the cells' surroundings optimal, allowing metabolism to continue reliably and freeing the animal from being controlled by external changes.
questions.explanation: Cells and enzymes need stable conditions to function.

questions.question: Name the three components of a homeostatic control system.
questions.answer: The three components are: (i) a receptor (sensor) that detects the change in the regulated variable; (ii) a control centre (integrator), often in the brain or an endocrine gland, that compares the information against the set point and decides on the response; and (iii) an effector (a muscle or gland) that carries out the response to restore the set point.
questions.explanation: Receptor, control centre, effector.

questions.question: Explain negative feedback with an example.
questions.answer: In negative feedback the response opposes the original change and pushes the variable back towards its set point, giving stability. For example, when blood glucose rises after a meal, the pancreas releases insulin, which lowers blood glucose again; when glucose falls, glucagon raises it. Because the response always counters the change, the variable oscillates gently around the set point. Most homeostatic controls - temperature, glucose, water balance and pH - use negative feedback.
questions.explanation: Response opposes change; e.g. insulin lowering raised glucose.

questions.question: Give two examples of positive feedback in the body and state why it is used only briefly.
questions.answer: Two examples of positive feedback are: (i) the surge of oxytocin during childbirth, which intensifies uterine contractions until the baby is delivered; and (ii) the cascade of clotting factors during blood clotting. (The rising phase of a nerve impulse is another example.) In each, the response reinforces the original change. Positive feedback is inherently unstable, so it is used only briefly to drive a process rapidly to completion and is then switched off by an external event, such as birth.
questions.explanation: Childbirth and blood clotting; unstable so used briefly.

questions.question: Name the four ways in which the body exchanges heat with its surroundings.
questions.answer: Heat is exchanged with the surroundings by four physical routes: (i) radiation - emission of heat as infrared waves; (ii) conduction - transfer of heat to objects in direct contact; (iii) convection - transfer of heat to moving air or water; and (iv) evaporation - loss of heat when water such as sweat evaporates. Body temperature stays constant when heat gained equals heat lost.
questions.explanation: Radiation, conduction, convection, evaporation.

questions.question: How does an ectotherm regulate its body temperature?
questions.answer: An ectotherm (poikilotherm) cannot generate enough internal heat to keep a constant temperature, so its body temperature varies with the environment. It regulates temperature mainly by behaviour: it basks in the sun or on warm rocks to gain heat, and moves into shade, burrows or water to cool down. In this way a lizard, for example, keeps its temperature within a workable range without internal heat production.
questions.explanation: Behavioural regulation - basking and seeking shade.

questions.question: Describe the role of the hypothalamus in thermoregulation.
questions.answer: The hypothalamus in the brain acts as the body's thermostat. It contains a thermoregulatory centre that senses the temperature of the blood flowing through it and also receives signals from temperature receptors in the skin. It compares the body temperature with the set point (about 37 C) and, by negative feedback, triggers the appropriate responses - heat-conserving responses (such as vasoconstriction and shivering) if the body is too cold, and heat-losing responses (such as vasodilation and sweating) if it is too hot.
questions.explanation: Hypothalamus senses and compares temperature, triggers responses.

questions.question: List the body's responses to a rise in body temperature.
questions.answer: When body temperature rises above the set point, the hypothalamus triggers responses that lose heat: (i) the skin arterioles dilate (vasodilation), so more warm blood flows near the surface and heat radiates away, flushing the skin; (ii) the sweat glands secrete sweat, whose evaporation cools the body; and (iii) behaviour changes, such as seeking shade and reducing activity. These form a negative-feedback loop that returns the temperature to normal.
questions.explanation: Vasodilation, sweating, behavioural cooling.

questions.question: Explain how the body conserves and generates heat in cold conditions.
questions.answer: In cold conditions the hypothalamus triggers responses that conserve and generate heat: skin arterioles constrict (vasoconstriction) so less warm blood reaches the surface and less heat is lost; shivering - rapid involuntary muscle contractions - generates extra heat; the hair-erector muscles raise the body hairs (goose bumps) to trap an insulating layer of air; sweating stops; and the thyroid and adrenal glands may raise the metabolic rate to produce more heat. Together these restore the normal temperature.
questions.explanation: Vasoconstriction, shivering, hair erection, raised metabolism.

questions.question: What is fever, and how is it produced?
questions.answer: Fever is a controlled raising of the body's temperature above the normal set point. During an infection, chemicals called pyrogens are released; these act on the hypothalamus and RAISE its set point above 37 C. The body then uses its normal heat-gaining responses (such as shivering and vasoconstriction) to reach and hold the higher temperature, which is felt as fever. The raised temperature helps fight pathogens. When the infection is overcome the set point returns to normal and the extra heat is lost by sweating.
questions.explanation: Pyrogens raise the hypothalamic set point during infection.

questions.question: What is osmoregulation?
questions.answer: Osmoregulation is the homeostatic control of the water and salt (solute) content of the body fluids - that is, the regulation of their osmotic concentration. It keeps the internal environment neither too concentrated nor too dilute, so that cells neither shrink by losing water nor swell and burst by gaining it. In mammals the kidney is the principal osmoregulatory organ.
questions.explanation: Control of water and salt (osmotic) balance.

questions.question: How does the kidney help in osmoregulation?
questions.answer: The kidney regulates the water and salt balance of the blood. It filters the blood and then selectively reabsorbs water and salts back into it, adjusting the volume and concentration of the urine so that the blood's osmotic concentration stays constant. When the body has too little water, the kidney (under ADH) reabsorbs more water and passes a small volume of concentrated urine; when there is excess water, it passes a large volume of dilute urine. Aldosterone adjusts sodium reabsorption to control salt balance.
questions.explanation: Filtration plus selective reabsorption adjust urine volume and concentration.

questions.question: Compare osmoregulation in a freshwater fish and a marine bony fish.
questions.answer: A freshwater fish lives in water more dilute than its body fluids, so water constantly enters by osmosis and salts tend to be lost; it copes by producing large amounts of dilute urine and actively taking up salts through its gills. A marine bony fish lives in water saltier than its body fluids, so it tends to lose water and gain salt; it drinks sea water, excretes excess salt through its gills, and passes only a small amount of concentrated urine. Thus the two face opposite osmotic problems and solve them in opposite ways.
questions.explanation: Freshwater: gains water, dilute urine, takes up salt; marine: loses water, drinks sea water, excretes salt.

questions.question: How do terrestrial animals conserve water?
questions.answer: Terrestrial animals face the constant danger of drying out (desiccation), so they have several water-conserving adaptations. They have waterproof skins or cuticles that reduce evaporation; they produce concentrated urine (aided by ADH, which increases water reabsorption in the kidney); and many excrete their nitrogenous waste as insoluble uric acid, which needs very little water to remove. Behaviour, such as staying in burrows during the heat of the day, also reduces water loss.
questions.explanation: Waterproof skin, concentrated urine, uric acid excretion.

questions.question: Name the two hormones that regulate blood glucose and state their source.
questions.answer: Blood glucose is regulated by insulin and glucagon. Both are secreted by the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas: insulin from the beta cells and glucagon from the alpha cells. Insulin lowers blood glucose and glucagon raises it, and together they keep the level steady by negative feedback.
questions.explanation: Insulin and glucagon from the pancreatic islets of Langerhans.

questions.question: Explain what happens to blood glucose control after a carbohydrate-rich meal.
questions.answer: After a carbohydrate-rich meal, the blood glucose level rises as sugars are absorbed from the gut. The beta cells of the pancreas detect the rise and release INSULIN. Insulin lowers blood glucose by promoting the uptake of glucose into body cells and its storage in the liver and muscles as glycogen (glycogenesis), and by promoting its conversion to fat. As glucose is taken up and stored, the level falls back towards normal, and insulin secretion then decreases. This is negative feedback.
questions.explanation: Rising glucose triggers insulin, which stores glucose as glycogen and lowers the level.

questions.question: How is the pH of blood kept constant?
questions.answer: Human blood is kept close to pH 7.4 in three ways. First, buffers in the blood - chiefly the bicarbonate buffer system, together with proteins and phosphates - resist pH changes by mopping up excess acid or base. Second, the lungs remove carbon dioxide; since dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid, breathing it out removes acid, and the breathing rate is adjusted to control it. Third, the kidneys provide slow, long-term control by excreting excess hydrogen ions in the urine and managing bicarbonate. Together these hold blood pH within about 7.35 to 7.45.
questions.explanation: Buffers, lungs (remove CO2) and kidneys (excrete H+).

questions.question: Describe the homeostatic roles of the liver.
questions.answer: The liver has many homeostatic roles: it regulates blood glucose by storing excess glucose as glycogen and releasing glucose when needed; it deaminates excess amino acids and converts the toxic ammonia produced into much less toxic urea for excretion; it stores iron, vitamins and glycogen; it produces plasma proteins such as albumin (which maintains blood osmotic pressure) and clotting factors; it detoxifies drugs, alcohol and other poisons; and it generates heat that helps thermoregulation.
questions.explanation: Glucose store, urea formation, plasma proteins, detoxification, heat.

questions.question: How does excretion contribute to homeostasis?
questions.answer: Excretion is central to homeostasis, not merely a way of throwing out rubbish. By removing nitrogenous wastes (urea, uric acid), the excretory system - chiefly the kidneys - clears toxic substances from the blood. At the same time, by adjusting how much water, salt and hydrogen ion it removes, it controls the water balance, the salt balance and the pH of the internal environment. Thus excretion keeps several key variables of the internal environment constant.
questions.explanation: Excretion removes wastes and regulates water, salt and pH balance.

questions.question: What is diabetes mellitus, and how does it illustrate homeostatic failure?
questions.answer: Diabetes mellitus is a disorder in which the control of blood glucose fails because insulin is lacking or ineffective. Without effective insulin, glucose is not taken up and stored properly, so blood glucose rises dangerously high (hyperglycaemia) and spills into the urine, causing thirst, excessive urination and, in the long term, damage to blood vessels, nerves, eyes and kidneys. It illustrates homeostatic failure because a normal negative-feedback control system (insulin lowering raised glucose) has broken down, so the regulated variable is no longer held near its set point.
questions.explanation: Failure of the insulin-glucose negative-feedback loop; glucose stays high.

questions.question: Explain the concept of homeostasis, its importance, and describe the internal environment. Mention the work of Claude Bernard and Walter Cannon.
questions.answer:
Homeostasis is the maintenance of a constant internal environment in the body despite changes in the external surroundings. It is a dynamic steady state: variables such as temperature, water content, salt concentration, pH and glucose are held within narrow limits around a set point by continuous self-regulating adjustments, rather than being frozen at a single value.

Its importance lies in the sensitivity of cells. Enzymes and other proteins work properly only within a narrow range of conditions and are damaged outside them. Because the body's cells are bathed in the internal environment, keeping that environment constant keeps the cells' surroundings optimal, so metabolism can continue reliably. This constancy frees the animal from being a slave to its surroundings.

The internal environment is the extracellular fluid that surrounds the cells. It has three connected parts: blood plasma (fluid in the vessels), tissue (interstitial) fluid (which directly bathes the cells), and lymph (excess tissue fluid drained into lymphatic vessels). Cells exchange materials with the tissue fluid, which exchanges with blood, which exchanges with the outside world through the lungs, gut, kidneys and skin.

The French physiologist Claude Bernard first recognised the constant internal environment, which he called the 'milieu interieur', and said its constancy is the condition for a free and independent life. Later the American physiologist Walter Cannon studied how the body actively defends this constancy and coined the term 'homeostasis'.
questions.explanation: Definition, dynamic steady state, importance, internal environment (plasma/tissue fluid/lymph), Bernard and Cannon.

questions.question: Describe how homeostatic control systems work. Compare negative and positive feedback with examples.
questions.answer:
Homeostasis works through control systems built on the principle of feedback. Every control system has three components: a RECEPTOR (sensor) that detects a change in the regulated variable; a CONTROL CENTRE (integrator), often in the brain or an endocrine gland, that compares the information against the set point and decides on the response; and an EFFECTOR (a muscle or gland) that carries out the response to restore the set point.

In NEGATIVE FEEDBACK the response OPPOSES the original change, pushing the variable back towards the set point. If the variable rises, the response lowers it; if it falls, the response raises it. The result is stability, with the variable oscillating gently around the set point. A simple analogy is a thermostat and heater: the heater switches on when the room is cold and off when it is warm enough. Almost all homeostatic controls - temperature, blood glucose, water balance, blood pressure and pH - use negative feedback. For example, when blood glucose rises, insulin lowers it; when it falls, glucagon raises it.

In POSITIVE FEEDBACK the response REINFORCES the original change, driving the variable further from its starting point. It is used when a process must be pushed rapidly to completion. Examples include the surge of oxytocin that intensifies uterine contractions during childbirth until the baby is delivered, the cascade of clotting factors during blood clotting, and the rising phase of a nerve impulse. Because positive feedback is inherently unstable, it is used only briefly and is usually shut off by an external event, such as birth.
questions.explanation: Receptor/control centre/effector; negative opposes (glucose, thermostat); positive reinforces (childbirth, clotting).

questions.question: Explain thermoregulation. Distinguish endotherms from ectotherms and describe how heat is exchanged and controlled.
questions.answer:
Thermoregulation is the homeostatic control of body temperature. It matters because the enzymes that run metabolism work best within a narrow range of temperature; too cold and reactions slow, too hot and proteins denature.

Animals are classified by how they manage temperature. ENDOTHERMS (homeotherms, 'warm-blooded' animals) - birds and mammals - generate heat internally from their own metabolism and keep their body temperature nearly constant regardless of the surroundings; human core temperature is about 37 C. ECTOTHERMS (poikilotherms, 'cold-blooded' animals) - fishes, amphibians, reptiles and invertebrates - rely mainly on external heat, so their body temperature varies with the environment; they regulate behaviourally, for example by basking in the sun or moving into shade.

Heat is exchanged with the surroundings by four routes: radiation (emission as infrared waves), conduction (transfer to objects in contact), convection (transfer to moving air or water), and evaporation (loss of heat as water such as sweat evaporates). Body temperature stays constant when heat gained equals heat lost.

In mammals the SKIN is the main heat-exchange organ and the HYPOTHALAMUS is the thermostat. The hypothalamus senses the temperature of the blood and of the skin, compares it with the set point, and by negative feedback triggers heat-conserving responses when the body is cold (vasoconstriction, shivering, hair erection) and heat-losing responses when it is hot (vasodilation, sweating).
questions.explanation: Definition; endotherm vs ectotherm; four heat routes; skin and hypothalamus; feedback responses.

questions.question: Describe in detail how the human body responds to heat and to cold to keep its temperature constant.
questions.answer:
The human body keeps its core temperature near 37 C by negative feedback controlled by the hypothalamus, which senses blood temperature and skin signals and drives responses through the skin and other effectors.

RESPONSES TO COLD (aim: gain and conserve heat). When the body temperature falls, (i) the skin arterioles constrict (vasoconstriction), so less warm blood reaches the surface and less heat is lost; (ii) shivering begins - rapid involuntary muscle contractions that release heat; (iii) the hair-erector muscles raise the body hairs (goose bumps), trapping an insulating layer of air; (iv) sweating stops; and (v) the thyroid and adrenal glands may raise the metabolic rate to generate more heat.

RESPONSES TO HEAT (aim: lose heat). When the body temperature rises, (i) the skin arterioles dilate (vasodilation), so more warm blood flows near the surface and heat radiates away, flushing the skin; (ii) the sweat glands secrete sweat, whose evaporation cools the body; and (iii) behaviour changes, such as seeking shade and reducing activity.

In each case the response opposes the change: cooling triggers heat gain and warming triggers heat loss, so the temperature is returned to its set point and the responses are then switched off. This is a clear example of negative feedback keeping a variable constant.
questions.explanation: Cold: vasoconstriction, shivering, hair erection, raised metabolism; heat: vasodilation, sweating; negative feedback.

questions.question: Explain osmoregulation in humans, including the roles of the kidney, ADH and aldosterone, and compare osmoregulation in different environments.
questions.answer:
Osmoregulation is the homeostatic control of the water and salt content of the body fluids - keeping their osmotic concentration steady so that cells neither shrink nor swell. In humans the KIDNEY is the principal osmoregulatory organ: it filters the blood and then selectively reabsorbs water and salts, adjusting the volume and concentration of urine to keep the blood's osmotic concentration constant.

Two hormones fine-tune this by negative feedback. ADH (antidiuretic hormone) from the posterior pituitary is released when the blood becomes too concentrated; osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the rise and increase ADH, which makes the collecting ducts more permeable to water so that more water is reabsorbed and a small volume of concentrated urine is passed. When the blood is too dilute, ADH falls and a large volume of dilute urine is passed. ALDOSTERONE from the adrenal cortex controls salt balance by promoting the reabsorption of sodium ions (and with them water), which also regulates blood volume and pressure.

Different environments pose different problems. FRESHWATER animals live in surroundings more dilute than their body fluids, so water enters by osmosis and salts are lost; they make large amounts of dilute urine and take up salts through the gills. MARINE bony fishes live in saltier water, so they lose water and gain salt; they drink sea water, excrete salt through the gills and pass little concentrated urine. TERRESTRIAL animals risk drying out; they use waterproof skins, produce concentrated urine and often excrete uric acid, which needs little water.
questions.explanation: Kidney; ADH (water) and aldosterone (Na+); freshwater vs marine vs terrestrial.

questions.question: Explain how blood glucose and blood pH are regulated in the human body.
questions.answer:
REGULATION OF BLOOD GLUCOSE. Glucose is the body's main fuel and the brain depends on a steady supply; the normal fasting level is about 70-110 mg per 100 mL. Two hormones from the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas control it by negative feedback. When blood glucose RISES (after a meal), the beta cells release INSULIN, which lowers it by promoting glucose uptake into cells and its storage in the liver and muscles as glycogen (glycogenesis) and its conversion to fat. When blood glucose FALLS (during fasting), the alpha cells release GLUCAGON, which raises it by stimulating the liver to break down glycogen into glucose (glycogenolysis) and make new glucose. Because insulin lowers and glucagon raises glucose, they are antagonistic, and their balanced action keeps the level steady. Failure of this control (lack or ineffectiveness of insulin) causes diabetes mellitus.

REGULATION OF BLOOD pH. Human blood is kept near pH 7.4. It is defended in three ways: (i) buffers, chiefly the bicarbonate buffer system with proteins and phosphates, resist pH changes by absorbing excess acid or base; (ii) the lungs remove carbon dioxide - since dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid, breathing it out removes acid, and the breathing rate is adjusted to control it; and (iii) the kidneys give slow, long-term control by excreting excess hydrogen ions and managing bicarbonate. Together these keep blood pH within about 7.35 to 7.45.
questions.explanation: Glucose: insulin lowers, glucagon raises (antagonistic); pH: buffers, lungs, kidneys.

questions.question: Describe the homeostatic roles of the liver and of excretion by the kidneys.
questions.answer:
The LIVER is one of the most versatile homeostatic organs. Its roles include: (i) regulating blood glucose by storing excess glucose as glycogen and releasing glucose when needed, under the control of insulin and glucagon; (ii) deaminating excess amino acids and converting the toxic ammonia produced into much less toxic urea (through the urea cycle) for excretion; (iii) storing iron, vitamins and glycogen; (iv) producing plasma proteins such as albumin, which maintains blood osmotic pressure, and clotting factors; (v) detoxifying drugs, alcohol and other poisons; and (vi) generating heat that helps thermoregulation.

EXCRETION by the kidneys is itself a homeostatic process. By removing nitrogenous wastes (urea and uric acid), excess salts, water and hydrogen ions, the kidneys simultaneously control the water balance, the salt balance and the pH of the internal environment, in addition to clearing toxic wastes from the blood. The kidney filters the blood and then selectively reabsorbs useful substances and water, so that the composition of the internal environment is kept constant. Thus excretion is not merely disposal of wastes but a central pillar of homeostasis.
questions.explanation: Liver: glucose, urea, plasma proteins, detoxification, heat; kidneys: water, salt, pH, waste removal.

questions.question: Analyse how the breakdown of homeostatic control leads to disorders. Discuss at least three examples.
questions.answer:
Homeostasis depends on control systems that hold each variable near its set point. When such a control system breaks down, the variable moves outside its safe range and disease results; these are disorders of homeostatic failure.

(1) DIABETES MELLITUS is a failure of blood-glucose control. Insulin is lacking or ineffective, so the negative-feedback loop that normally lowers raised glucose fails. Blood glucose stays dangerously high (hyperglycaemia) and spills into the urine, causing thirst, excessive urination and, over time, damage to blood vessels, nerves, eyes and kidneys.

(2) FAILURE OF TEMPERATURE CONTROL. If the thermoregulatory responses are overwhelmed - by extreme cold or heat - the body temperature moves outside its set range. HYPOTHERMIA (dangerously low temperature) slows metabolism and can stop the heart; HYPERTHERMIA or heat stroke (dangerously high temperature) can denature proteins and damage the brain.

(3) DISTURBANCE OF BLOOD pH. If the buffers, lungs and kidneys cannot keep pH near 7.4, ACIDOSIS (blood too acidic) or ALKALOSIS (blood too alkaline) develops, disturbing enzyme activity and nerve and muscle function.

(4) KIDNEY FAILURE disrupts the balance of water, salts, pH and wastes, so several variables of the internal environment drift at once.

In each case a specific control system has broken down, showing by its consequences how vital continuous homeostatic regulation is to life.
questions.explanation: Diabetes (glucose), hypothermia/heat stroke (temperature), acidosis/alkalosis (pH), kidney failure - each a control failure.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The cells of the human body are never in direct contact with the outside world. They are surrounded by a fluid that supplies them with oxygen and nutrients and removes their wastes. Claude Bernard called this fluid the 'milieu interieur' and said that its constancy is the condition for a free and independent life. Walter Cannon later coined a term for the processes that keep it steady.

(a) What is the fluid that surrounds the cells collectively called?
(b) Name its three parts.
(c) What term did Walter Cannon coin?
(d) Why is a constant internal environment important for the cells?
questions.answer: (a) The fluid is collectively called the internal environment (the extracellular fluid). (b) Its three parts are blood plasma, tissue (interstitial) fluid and lymph. (c) Walter Cannon coined the term 'homeostasis'. (d) A constant internal environment is important because cells and their enzymes work properly only within a narrow range of conditions; keeping the surrounding fluid steady keeps conditions optimal for metabolism and frees the animal from control by external changes.
questions.explanation: Internal environment; plasma/tissue fluid/lymph; homeostasis; cells need stable conditions.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A homeostatic control system has a receptor that detects a change, a control centre that compares it with a set point, and an effector that responds. In one type of control the response reverses the change; in another, rarer type the response reinforces the change and drives a process to completion.

(a) Name the three components of a control system.
(b) What is the type of control in which the response reverses the change called?
(c) Give one example of the rarer type of feedback.
(d) Why is the rarer type used only briefly?
questions.answer: (a) The three components are the receptor, the control centre and the effector. (b) It is called negative feedback. (c) An example of the rarer type (positive feedback) is childbirth, in which oxytocin intensifies uterine contractions; blood clotting is another. (d) Positive feedback is inherently unstable, so it is used only briefly to drive a process rapidly to completion and is then switched off by an external event such as birth.
questions.explanation: Receptor/control centre/effector; negative feedback; childbirth; unstable so brief.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A lizard begins its day cold and sluggish. It climbs onto a sunny rock and lies still until it is warm and active. Later, when the rock becomes very hot, it moves into the shade. In contrast, a nearby dog keeps the same body temperature all day, panting when it is hot.

(a) Is the lizard an endotherm or an ectotherm?
(b) How does the lizard control its temperature?
(c) To which group does the dog belong?
(d) Name the brain region that acts as the dog's thermostat.
questions.answer: (a) The lizard is an ectotherm (poikilotherm). (b) It controls its temperature behaviourally - basking on the sunny rock to warm up and moving into shade to cool down - because it cannot generate enough internal heat. (c) The dog is an endotherm (homeotherm), keeping a constant body temperature by internal metabolic heat. (d) The brain region acting as the thermostat is the hypothalamus.
questions.explanation: Ectotherm; behavioural regulation; endotherm; hypothalamus.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A hiker is caught in cold, windy weather without warm clothing. Soon she notices that her skin has gone pale, she has 'goose bumps', and she starts to shiver uncontrollably.

(a) Why has her skin gone pale?
(b) What causes the 'goose bumps' and how do they help?
(c) How does shivering help her?
(d) Which control centre coordinates all these responses?
questions.answer: (a) Her skin has gone pale because the skin arterioles have constricted (vasoconstriction), reducing blood flow to the surface so that less heat is lost. (b) The goose bumps are caused by contraction of the hair-erector muscles, which raise the body hairs; this traps an insulating layer of air next to the skin and reduces heat loss. (c) Shivering is rapid involuntary muscle contraction that generates extra heat to warm the body. (d) All these responses are coordinated by the hypothalamus, the body's thermostat.
questions.explanation: Vasoconstriction (pale); hair erection traps air; shivering makes heat; hypothalamus coordinates.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

After playing football on a hot afternoon, a boy sweats heavily and drinks very little water. That evening he notices that he passes only a small amount of dark, concentrated urine.

(a) Why has his blood become more concentrated?
(b) Which hormone will have increased in his blood?
(c) How does this hormone produce concentrated urine?
(d) What would happen to the urine if he later drank a large amount of water?
questions.answer: (a) His blood has become more concentrated because he has lost a lot of water in sweat and replaced very little, raising the osmotic concentration of the blood. (b) The level of ADH (antidiuretic hormone) will have increased. (c) ADH makes the kidney collecting ducts more permeable to water, so more water is reabsorbed into the blood and only a small volume of concentrated urine is produced. (d) If he later drank a large amount of water, the blood would become dilute, ADH would fall, and he would pass a large volume of dilute urine.
questions.explanation: Water loss concentrates blood; ADH rises; more water reabsorbed; dilute urine after drinking.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

After eating a large plate of rice, a person's blood glucose rises. Within a couple of hours it has returned to normal. Several hours later, having eaten nothing more, the level begins to fall, but it is quickly restored.

(a) Which hormone brought the raised glucose back to normal after the meal?
(b) How does this hormone lower blood glucose?
(c) Which hormone restores the level when it falls during fasting?
(d) Why are these two hormones described as antagonistic?
questions.answer: (a) Insulin brought the raised glucose back to normal after the meal. (b) Insulin lowers blood glucose by promoting the uptake of glucose into cells and its storage in the liver and muscles as glycogen (glycogenesis), and its conversion to fat. (c) Glucagon restores the level when it falls during fasting, by stimulating the liver to break down glycogen into glucose. (d) They are antagonistic because they act in opposite directions - insulin lowers blood glucose while glucagon raises it - and their balanced action keeps the level steady.
questions.explanation: Insulin lowers (stores glycogen); glucagon raises (breaks glycogen); opposite = antagonistic.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

During vigorous exercise, muscles produce extra carbon dioxide and acids, which tend to lower the pH of the blood. Yet a blood test still shows a pH close to 7.4. The person is also breathing much faster than at rest.

(a) What is the normal pH of blood?
(b) Name the chief buffer system that resists the pH change.
(c) How does faster breathing help to control blood pH?
(d) Which organ provides the slow, long-term control of pH?
questions.answer: (a) The normal pH of blood is about 7.4 (within roughly 7.35 to 7.45). (b) The chief buffer system that resists the change is the bicarbonate buffer system. (c) Faster breathing removes more carbon dioxide from the blood; since dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid, breathing it out removes acid and prevents the pH from falling. (d) The kidneys provide the slow, long-term control of pH, by excreting excess hydrogen ions and managing bicarbonate.
questions.explanation: pH 7.4; bicarbonate buffer; faster breathing removes CO2/acid; kidneys give long-term control.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The liver is often called the body's 'chemical factory'. Among many jobs, it stores a carbohydrate, deals with the toxic ammonia formed from excess amino acids, makes proteins found in the blood plasma, and breaks down alcohol and drugs.

(a) Name the carbohydrate stored in the liver.
(b) Into what less toxic substance does the liver convert ammonia?
(c) Name one plasma protein made by the liver and state its homeostatic role.
(d) What name is given to the liver's breakdown of alcohol and drugs?
questions.answer: (a) The carbohydrate stored in the liver is glycogen. (b) The liver converts toxic ammonia into much less toxic urea. (c) One plasma protein made by the liver is albumin, which maintains the osmotic pressure of the blood (another is fibrinogen/clotting factors, which help blood clotting). (d) The breakdown of alcohol and drugs is called detoxification.
questions.explanation: Glycogen; urea; albumin (osmotic pressure); detoxification.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A patient feels very thirsty, passes large amounts of urine, and feels tired. A blood test shows a very high glucose level, and glucose is found in the urine. The doctor explains that a hormone from the pancreas is either lacking or not working properly.

(a) Name the disorder the patient is likely to have.
(b) Which hormone is lacking or ineffective?
(c) Why does glucose appear in the urine?
(d) Explain how this illustrates a failure of homeostasis.
questions.answer: (a) The patient is likely to have diabetes mellitus. (b) The hormone that is lacking or ineffective is insulin. (c) Glucose appears in the urine because the blood glucose is so high that the kidney cannot reabsorb all of it, so the excess spills into the urine. (d) It illustrates a failure of homeostasis because the normal negative-feedback control that lowers raised blood glucose (insulin acting to store glucose as glycogen) has broken down, so blood glucose is no longer held near its set point but rises dangerously high.
questions.explanation: Diabetes mellitus; insulin; excess glucose spills into urine; broken glucose feedback loop.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

An elderly man is brought indoors after being lost outdoors on a freezing night. His body temperature is only 33 C, he is confused, and his shivering has stopped. The doctor warns that his temperature control has been overwhelmed.

(a) What is the name of this dangerously low body temperature?
(b) Normally, which response would generate heat, and why has it stopped?
(c) Which brain region normally controls body temperature?
(d) Why is this condition described as a failure of homeostasis?
questions.answer: (a) The dangerously low body temperature is called hypothermia. (b) Shivering would normally generate heat by rapid muscle contraction, but as the body cools too far the control system is overwhelmed and shivering stops, so heat production fails. (c) The hypothalamus normally controls body temperature, acting as the thermostat. (d) It is described as a failure of homeostasis because the temperature-control system can no longer keep the body temperature at its set point of about 37 C; the temperature has drifted far outside the safe range, which is dangerous to life.
questions.explanation: Hypothermia; shivering stops as control is overwhelmed; hypothalamus; set point not maintained.
